lesson.body:
"Terroir" sounds fancy, but the idea is simple: a wine tastes of WHERE it grew. It's a French word (say "ter-WAHR") for the whole package of a place — the soil the vines dig into, the climate, how much sun a slope gets, the altitude, even the local know-how passed down over generations. Think of it like a tomato. One grown in your sunny backyard tastes different from a supermarket one, even though they're the same fruit. The place leaves its fingerprint.

That's why the SAME grape can taste totally different from two regions. A Chardonnay grape grown in cool, chalky northern France tastes lean and crisp; the same grape in warm, sunny California tastes riper and rounder. Same seed, different home, different flavor.

So terroir isn't magic or wine-snob mystery — it's just nature's recipe for that spot. When someone says a wine "shows its terroir," they simply mean you can taste where it came from. Next time, sip and ask: warm place or cool one?
outcomes: Define terroir as a wine's sense of place
Name what makes up a place's terroir
Explain why one grape tastes different in two places

deep_notes: The word comes from the French terre, meaning earth or land. The idea sits at the heart of French wine law: most of France's classic wines are named after their place, not their grape. That system is called appellation d'origine contrôlée (AOC), a protected place name with its own rules. So a label that says Chablis tells you where the wine is from, and you are expected to know the grape inside is Chardonnay.

Pros call the direction a slope faces its aspect. In the Northern Hemisphere, south-facing slopes catch the most sun, which helps grapes ripen in cool places such as Germany's Mosel valley. Altitude works the other way: the air cools by about 0.6°C for every 100 metres you climb. Soil matters mostly through water. Well-drained gravel or slate keeps roots from getting waterlogged, and stony soils can hold the day's warmth.

The classic example is Chablis, at the cool northern tip of Burgundy, where Chardonnay grows on limestone-rich soils. It usually tastes of green apple, lemon and wet stone. Chardonnay from warm parts of California leans towards ripe peach, pineapple and mango. Part of that gap is winemaking too: many Californian versions are aged in oak barrels, which add vanilla and toast, while most Chablis sees little or no new oak.

Terroir is easiest to taste side by side. Burgundy is the classic test case: neighbouring plots of Pinot Noir, sometimes only a path apart, are ranked and priced very differently. Burgundians call a named vineyard plot a climat. Many everyday wines blend grapes from across a whole region, which smooths out the stamp of any one spot, so single-vineyard wines usually show their terroir most clearly.

deeper.body: Soil works mainly through water and warmth. On Bordeaux's Left Bank, gravel drains fast and holds heat, helping the late-ripening Cabernet Sauvignon ripen fully. The Right Bank has more clay, which stays cooler and holds water, and that suits Merlot, which ripens earlier. So soil rarely adds a flavour directly. It decides which grape does best there and how well it ripens.
deeper.title: Gravel for Cabernet, clay for Merlot

opts: Gravel adds a stony flavour straight into the grapes
Gravel keeps the roots cool and wet
Gravel drains well and holds heat, helping a late ripener
Gravel makes it ripen earlier than Merlot
deeper.q: Why does Cabernet Sauvignon do well on the gravel of Bordeaux's Left Bank?
deeper.why: Cabernet Sauvignon ripens late, so it needs all the help it can get. Warm, fast-draining gravel gives it that help.

deeper.body: Nearby water is a hidden part of terroir. Big lakes and rivers warm up and cool down slowly, so they soften frosts in spring and autumn. Cold oceans can do the opposite job: along the California coast, fog and sea breezes from the chilly Pacific cool the vineyards, keeping acidity fresh in grapes that would otherwise ripen too fast.
deeper.title: Water as a heater and a fan

opts: Cool the vines with fog and sea breezes
deeper.q: Which of these can a nearby body of water do for a vineyard?
deeper.why: Lakes and rivers even out temperatures, which softens frost. A cold ocean sends in fog and breezes that cool the vines.

deeper.body: The human side of terroir runs deep in Burgundy. From the Middle Ages, Cistercian monks farmed its slopes and noted which plots gave the best wine year after year. They walled in one prized vineyard, Clos de Vougeot, which still exists. A clos is a walled vineyard. Their work helped lay the ground for today's ranking: grand cru at the top, then premier cru, then village wines.
deeper.title: The monks who mapped Burgundy

deeper.q: In Burgundy, premier cru vineyards rank above grand cru vineyards.
deeper.why: Grand cru is the top rank. Premier cru comes second, even though its name means "first growth", and village wines come after that.

bank.why: If a place shows in the wine every year, the vineyard name on a label tells you something.

bank.why: Terroir covers the fixed features of a place, which show up year after year.

bank.key: Minerality is a tasting word for a stony, flinty or salty impression.
bank.q: What does the tasting word 'minerality' describe?
bank.remember: Minerality is a feeling, not a pebble.

bank.remember: Struck match: a cellar note, not a rock.

v2.body:
In 1855, the same year Bordeaux ranked its châteaux, a Dijon doctor called **Jules Lavalle** published a book that ranked the vineyards of Burgundy's Côte d'Or plot by plot, village by village. In 1861 Beaune's agriculture committee built its own classification largely on his, and it helped shape the Grand Cru vineyards fixed by law in the 1930s. Lavalle bet that each plot's character would hold, year after year.

Terroir (say teh-RWAHR) is a place shaping its wine through climate, soil, slope and people. This lesson tests the parts fixed to the site, which stay the same year after year: soil and rock, slope, nearby water, and which grape suits it. Climate, a region's long-term warmth, gets the next lesson; one year's weather, the **vintage**, the one after.

Soil works like plumbing, not seasoning: it rarely adds flavour directly. It decides how fast rain drains away (gravel and slate drain fast), how much water is stored for summer (chalk and clay hold a reserve), how much warmth stones such as Châteauneuf's galets soak up by day, and how fertile the ground is: poor soil keeps a vine less leafy and its crop small. In Bordeaux Gérard Seguin, and later **Cornelis van Leeuwen**, found that water was the key. A vine **mildly short of water** stops growing shoots early and ripens small berries with more colour and tannin, ideal for red wine. Severe drought stalls ripening.

Then there is **minerality**, a tasting word for a stony, flinty or salty impression. It sounds like the taste of rock, but geologists such as Alex Maltman point out that wine holds only tiny traces of minerals, and there is no evidence that you can taste the rock. Studies suggest tasters say 'mineral' for:
• quiet fruit (little obvious fruitiness)
• a struck-match or flinty smell, from **reduction**, a smell that builds when wine is kept away from air
• sharp acidity, though here the studies disagree

To taste terroir, change only the vineyard. Pour two wines from the same producer, grape and vintage but different plots, such as two Premier Crus from one estate. Wines from one year side by side make a horizontal tasting. A **single-vineyard** wine usually shows its place more clearly than a regional blend, which smooths out each plot's stamp.

Terroir is not only European: think of Coonawarra's strip of red terra rossa soil, the Gimblett Gravels on an old riverbed in Hawke's Bay, and Napa sub-regions such as Oakville.

People are part of it too. Over centuries growers matched grape to place: in 1395 Philip the Bold kept Burgundy's best slopes for Pinot Noir. The OIV's official definition of terroir, adopted in 2010, includes this shared know-how.
deep_notes: The doctor was Jules Lavalle, from Dijon, and he did not start from nothing. He drew heavily on an 1831 survey of the Côte d'Or by Denis Morelot, and he worked with owners and growers village by village. He ranked the plots within each village first, then across the whole slope, and his top rank in a village was called tête de cuvée. Many of his favourites became today's Grand Crus, though tasters still argue that some Premier Crus deserved promotion.

Climate is one of terroir's four parts, and in the wide sense it belongs there. This unit pulls the ideas apart because they are so often muddled. Terroir here is the site: its rock, its slope, its water and the choices of the people who farm it. Climate is the long-term average warmth and rain of the region around it. Vintage is how one year's weather departed from that average. A great site shows its character in warm and cool years alike, the bet Lavalle made.

Think of Bordeaux's gravel, Champagne's chalk, the Mosel's slate, Châteauneuf's galets. What links them is not their chemistry but their plumbing. A vine needs nitrogen and other nutrients, but only in modest amounts: rich, wet soil pushes it to grow leaves and a large, dilute crop. That is why so many great vineyards sit on thin, stony ground that would make a poor vegetable garden.

Seguin studied the Médoc's soils in the 1970s and 1980s and found that many top sites were poor in nutrients, made up for by deep roots. He could find no link between wine quality and how much of any nutrient the soil held. Van Leeuwen and his colleagues later measured the water status of vines on different soils: early water stress limited berry size and raised colour, and sugar was highest when the shortage was mild. Too much stress shuts the leaves down.

Alex Maltman, an emeritus professor of earth sciences at Aberystwyth University, has made the case most clearly. Vines are built mostly from carbon, hydrogen and oxygen taken from air and water. Their nutrient minerals come largely through the soil's water and its humus, the decayed organic part, rather than straight from the rock, and fermentation changes the wine further. Solid rock gives off no smell either, so a stony aroma cannot come from the stones themselves.

Researchers including Wendy Parr in New Zealand found that Sauvignon Blancs judged low in fruity and green notes, and with struck-match notes, were more often called mineral; acidity on its own showed no clear link. Those flinty smells come from sulphur compounds formed in the cellar, and they show most when a wine has had little contact with air, for example under a screwcap. Tasters often disagree about which wines are mineral at all, so treat the word as a personal impression.

Burgundy is the classic test bench, because most plots grow a single grape, Pinot Noir or Chardonnay, and many growers own several plots side by side. A village wine and a Premier Cru from the same cellar differ mainly in where the grapes grew. The same flight works with two German Rieslings from named vineyards, or two Barolos from different named sites. The opposite set, one wine across several years, is a vertical tasting: it shows the vintage, not the place.

New World terroir lines were often drawn by soil and argued over. Coonawarra's boundary took more than a decade of dispute and appeals from the 1990s, much of it about how far the red soil reached. In Hawke's Bay, the Gimblett Gravels district is marked out by its stony old riverbed. Napa nests over a dozen sub-regions such as Oakville inside its official Napa Valley area. Each line is a bet that the place shows in the glass, the same bet Lavalle made.

Know-how is the least visible part of terroir. Matching grape to site took centuries of trial and error in Europe, and the duke's choice of Pinot Noir in 1395 is one early example. Pruning, picking dates and cellar habits passed down in a village shape the wine too, which is why the OIV counts people in. Tasters call the result typicity: whether a wine tastes typical of its place.

deeper.body: From the 1970s Gérard Seguin studied the soils under the Médoc's finest estates. Many were poor in nutrients, yet their vines rooted deep. He found no link between wine quality and how much of any nutrient the soil held. What mattered was how the soil fed water to the vine: steadily and modestly, never too much. His work helped move terroir research away from soil chemistry and towards soil water.
deeper.title: Great Médoc soils are often poor ones

deeper.key: Seguin found the soil's water supply mattered, not its nutrient content.
opts: How they fed water to vines
deeper.q: What did Seguin find mattered most in the Médoc's best soils?
deeper.remember: Follow the water, not the nutrients.
deeper.why: It explains why great vineyards can sit on poor, stony ground.

deeper.body: The flinty, struck-match smell many tasters call mineral comes largely from sulphur compounds formed in the cellar, not from flint in the soil. One of them, benzenemethanethiol, smells of gunflint and is prized in some Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc. It forms best without air, so these notes show most in wines kept away from oxygen, as under a screwcap. The bottle's closure, not the vineyard's rock, can make a wine seem mineral.
deeper.title: Flint in the glass comes from the cellar

deeper.key: Flinty, struck-match smells come largely from sulphur compounds formed in the cellar.
deeper.q: Flinty smells in wine come straight from flint stones in the vineyard soil.
deeper.remember: Gunflint is made in the cellar.
deeper.why: They show most when a wine has had little air, which is why winemaking choices matter here.

deeper.body: Scientists at the University of California, Davis, sequenced the fungi and bacteria living on grapes from vineyards across California. The mix of microbes differed by region, by grape variety and by vintage, and it tracked local climate. They called the pattern microbial terroir. Since yeasts and bacteria drive fermentation, the local mix could shape flavour, though how much it shows in the finished wine is still being studied.
deeper.title: Microbes may be part of the place

deeper.key: The mix of microbes on grapes differed by region, grape variety and vintage.
opts: Every vineyard shares the same microbes
The mix differed by region and grape
Microbes on grapes die before harvest
Only red grapes carry any microbes
deeper.q: What did the UC Davis study of grape microbes find?
deeper.remember: Even the invisible life on grapes has an address.
deeper.why: Since microbes drive fermentation, a place's microbes may add to its stamp on the wine.

steps.body: Terroir includes the people. Their choices, tested over generations, decide which grape grows where. The OIV, wine's international body, includes this shared know-how in its official definition of terroir.
steps.stat: In 1395 Burgundy's duke kept its best slopes for Pinot Noir
steps.tip: Next time a region is famous for one grape, remember that people chose it, plot by plot.
steps.title: People matched grape to place over centuries

steps.key: Keep producer, grape and vintage the same and change only the vineyard plot.

steps.q: You want to taste terroir at home. Which pair works best?
steps.why: Then the only difference left in the glass is the place itself.

steps.key: Oakville is a sub-region inside Napa: a small place name inside a big one marks a more specific site.

steps.remember: Small name inside a big one: a terroir clue.
steps.why: Narrower place names point to a particular terroir, just as Burgundy's village and vineyard names do.

cards.back: Everything about a vineyard that stays the same year after year: climate, soil, slope and people.
A stony, flinty or salty impression in a wine, not the taste of the vineyard's rock.
A vine slightly short of water: fewer shoots, small berries, more colour and tannin.
A wine from one plot, which usually shows its place more clearly than a regional blend.
